An arch is a curved structure that spans — that is, bridges over — an opening or a gap. Picture a rainbow, or the letter U turned upside down. That graceful, rising-and-falling curve is the defining image of an arch.

The essential word here is curved. This is what separates an arch from a flat beam (which goes straight across an opening) or a simple rectangular frame. An arch bends as it rises on one side, reaches its peak, and curves back down on the other.
The Architectural Arch — The Main Meaning

When most people say "arch," they're talking about the architectural arch — a structure, typically built of stone, brick, or concrete, that curves over an opening and supports the weight above it.

You encounter arches constantly: the curved top of a church doorway, a bridge that arcs gracefully over a river, the entrance to a tunnel, the tall windows of an old cathedral. In every case, there is a gap below and a curved structure rising over it.

What makes the arch remarkable — and the reason builders have relied on it for thousands of years — is its extraordinary strength. When weight presses down on the top of an arch, the arch doesn't simply buckle as a flat beam might. Instead, it cleverly redirects that downward force outward and downward along its two curving sides, pushing into the walls or supports on either end. These supporting structures on either side are called abutments. Because of this clever redirection of force, an arch can support enormous loads — whole ceilings, entire bridges — while leaving a wide open space below.

The single most important piece of an arch is the keystone, the wedge-shaped stone placed at the very top center. It locks all the surrounding stones in place. Remove it, and the arch collapses. You'll often hear this word used beyond architecture — "the keystone of the agreement" — meaning the one element that holds everything else together. Now you know exactly where that image comes from.

A few terms you'll encounter when reading about arches:

The crown is the highest point of the arch — the top of the curve. The keystone sits here. The springing line is where the arch begins to curve upward from its supports. And the abutments (mentioned above) are the structures on either side that the arch leans into and relies on for stability. The arch doesn't stand on its own — it pushes outward, and the abutments push back, and that tension is what holds everything together.

Arches appear in different shapes, and each carries a distinct character and history.

Round (Semicircular) Arch: A smooth, perfect half-circle. The Romans mastered this form — their aqueducts, bridges, and public buildings are full of evenly rounded arches. This shape conveys solidity and authority.

Pointed Arch: Two curves that rise and meet at a sharp point at the top. This is the hallmark of Gothic architecture, the style of the great medieval cathedrals of Europe. The pointed arch lets builders create taller, slimmer openings and push weight more efficiently, which is why Gothic cathedrals can have such soaring height.

Horseshoe Arch: Wider and more deeply curved than a semicircular arch — it curves past the halfway point and narrows again at the bottom before ending, resembling a horseshoe. This is characteristic of Islamic architecture and can be seen in the mosques, palaces, and gateways of Morocco, Spain, Turkey, and across the Middle East.

Parabolic Arch: Follows a mathematical parabola — a slightly flattened curve. Modern engineers often use this shape in large bridges and roofs because it distributes weight with exceptional efficiency.

Triumphal Arch: A grand, freestanding arch built not as part of a building but as a standalone monument — usually to commemorate a military victory or a leader. The Romans built many of these. The most famous in the modern world is the Arc de Triomphe in Paris, France, standing alone at the center of a great boulevard.

Nature creates arches too. When wind, water, and time slowly erode rock over thousands of years, they can wear away the softer material underneath a harder rock layer, leaving a curved stone span — a natural arch. These are free-standing curved rock formations with open space beneath them. Arches National Park in Utah, USA, takes its name from the extraordinary number of these formations found there.

The human foot has an arch. Look at the inside of your foot — it doesn't rest flat against the ground along its entire length. The middle section curves upward. This curved inner section is called the arch of the foot. It acts as a natural spring or shock absorber, flexing slightly with each step to absorb impact and distribute your body weight efficiently as you walk or run.

Some people have a very low or absent foot arch — their foot is flatter against the ground — which is commonly called flat feet.
Extended Uses of "Arch" as a Noun

Because "arch" fundamentally means a curved shape that rises over something and comes back down, it gets used descriptively for any shape that resembles this:

"The arch of her eyebrow" refers to the natural curve of an eyebrow as it rises and falls across the brow. "The arch of the sky" describes the sky itself seen as a vast dome curving overhead. "The arch of a wave" captures that curling, cresting curve of a wave before it breaks.

In all these uses, the word carries the same core image: something that curves upward, spans a space, and descends on the other side.

An arch is a curved structure that spans an opening. Whether it's holding up a cathedral ceiling, crossing a river, slowly carved by wind into a rock formation, cushioning your footsteps from within your own foot, or traced in the curve of an eyebrow or across the wide sky — the word always returns to the same essential picture: a curve that rises, arcs over, and comes back down on the other side. Its power — whether structural or visual — comes precisely from that curve.
